Open

get_osm_data()

get_wiki_data()

get_wikidata()

    • Why: get_wikidata() returns one height per item (the maximum of the normalized SI value from p:P2048/psn:P2048/wikibase:quantityAmount) and drops qualifiers. Wikidata heights are sparse (15 of 788 items within 3 km of 417 E Fayette St, Baltimore) and sometimes wrong or ambiguous. Baltimore City Hall (Q805741) has one P2048 value, +51.27, with qualifier P459 (determination method) = Q791801; the SPARQL normalized value is 15.6 m, so the unit appears to be feet and the value does not describe the dome.
    • Starting point: tw_get_qualified_property() in https://github.com/elipousson/weirdunits/blob/main/R/tidywikidatar.R. It takes QIDs (or a data frame with a qid column) and a property ID, then returns a list with properties (value, unit via tw_get_property_with_details(), converted to a units object) and qualifiers (labelled with tw_get_label() and tw_get_property_label()).
    • Known problems to solve first:
      • tw_get_property_with_details() returned only id and p columns (no amount or unit) for Q805741, Q1383405 and Q3381384, while tw_get_qualifiers() worked. In the weirdunits helper this skips the unit join entirely, so unit_value is never created. Check whether this is a tidywikidatar 0.6.2 issue, a cache issue (tw_disable_cache() was on in testing), or a data issue, and consider reading the unit from SPARQL (psv:P2048/wikibase:quantityUnit) instead.
      • tw_get_qualifiers() takes one item and property pair at a time. For more than a handful of items this means many API calls, so enrich only a shortlist and enable the tidywikidatar cache (tw_enable_cache()).
      • Qualifiers worth keeping for height: P459 (determination method), P518 (applies to part, e.g. roof or spire), P585 (point in time).
    • Design options: (a) add an internal or exported helper such as get_wikidata_property() that takes qid and a property and returns tidy values plus qualifiers, with tidywikidatar in Suggests and check_installed(); or (b) skip tidywikidatar and extend the SPARQL query with OPTIONAL qualifier patterns (p:P2048/pq:P518, p:P2048/pq:P459) and return all height statements as list-columns. Option (b) is one request for all items; option (a) is more general.
    • Tests: use a canned response for offline tests and a live test (skipped offline and on CI) on Q805741, Q1383405 (100 Light Street) and Q3381384 (Phoenix Shot Tower).

General

Viewshed and landmark labelling (planning)

Goal: work out which landmarks are visible from a window (8th floor, 417 E Fayette St, Baltimore), then label them on a photo or generated illustration. Background, data checks and a candidate pipeline are in vignettes/viewshed.Rmd. Scripts used for the checks are in dev/. Status as of 2026-11-05: get_wikidata() and get_wiki_data() are done and committed; the open decision is how to build the surface model (DSM) used for occlusion.

What we know (details in the vignette):

  • OSM heights/levels cover only 3.1% of buildings within 3 km (7.3% in the 1 km core), mostly the tall towers. Overture adds almost nothing beyond OSM. Wikidata heights are sparse and sometimes wrong.
  • Two 3DEP lidar projects cover downtown. USGS_LPC_MD_PA_SandySupp_2014 (acquired 2014-12-15/16, leaf-off, ~8 points/m2) captures the City Hall dome (~70 m above ground).
  • terrainr::get_tiles() returned a keyless 1 m bare-earth DEM for a 500 m window in ~4 s (11 m at City Hall; lidar ground ~10.8 m).
  • elevatr 0.99.1 sources are aws, gl3, gl1, alos and srtm15plus (no direct 3DEP source).

Option 1: lidar DSM for the whole area (needs discussion)

Build a ground surface and a surface model from the 2014 3DEP point cloud.

  • Steps:
    1. Ground: terrainr::get_tiles(services = "elevation", resolution = 1) (see dev/terrainr_dem_test.R), reproject to EPSG:26985.
    2. Surface: pull EPT tiles for the study radius (dev/ept_pull.py), reproject from EPSG:3857, rasterize the highest return per 1 m cell after removing outliers (not by class code), and fill voids.
    3. Patch buildings built or demolished since 2014 using OSM height and building:levels (see the footprint-comparison note below).
  • Pros: captures domes, spires, bridges (such as the elevated highway in the northeast photo) and trees; real geometry rather than modeled heights; one keyless public source.
  • Cons:
    • 2014 vintage: newer buildings are missing and demolished ones remain.
    • Leaf-off (December) versus summer photos, so trees look thinner.
    • Download size: the 500 m test window was 22 MB and ~59 s serial. A rough linear extrapolation to a 3 km radius (~28 km2) is ~2.5 GB and ~2 hours serial (estimate, not tested; tile downloads can run in parallel).
    • Class codes are not reliable (buildings mostly class 17, class 18 includes ground-level points), so noise must be removed another way.
    • EPSG:3857 stretches horizontal distance by ~1.29 here; must reproject.
    • Currently depends on Python (laspy) outside the package.
  • Docs:
    • USGS 3DEP lidar on AWS: https://registry.opendata.aws/usgs-lidar/
    • Project index: https://usgs.entwine.io/boundaries/resources.geojson
    • Index tooling: https://github.com/hobuinc/usgs-lidar
    • EPT specification: https://entwine.io/en/latest/entwine-point-tile.html
    • laspy: https://laspy.readthedocs.io/
    • terrainr: https://docs.ropensci.org/terrainr/
  • Open questions: study radius needed for the far landmarks; whether MD_Baltimore_2008 is worth using for comparison; how well a leaf-off DSM matches the summer photos.

Option 2: replace the Python step with R tooling (needs discussion)

Keep the lidar approach but process points with lidR or {lasR} (or PDAL) so the workflow is R-only.

  • Pros:
    • {lasR} pipelines can produce DSM and DTM from a folder of point clouds (README example), including outlier removal, and read local or remote LAS, LAZ and COPC files.
    • lidR is on CRAN (4.3.3) with a book-length manual.
    • No Python or uv dependency for users.
  • Cons:
    • Neither package lists EPT as a supported format (checked READMEs and lidR NEWS only; not exhaustive). We would still fetch the EPT node LAZ tiles ourselves (as dev/ept_pull.py does) or find LAZ/COPC sources. The public usgs-lidar-public bucket is EPT; the raw LAZ bucket is requester-pays and needs AWS credentials.
    • {lasR} is not on CRAN (r-universe, version 0.21.4 on 2026-11-05), which complicates Suggests/Remotes.
    • PDAL (readers.ept) would read EPT directly but is a system dependency (brew install pdal; not installed here).
    • Not tested at all yet.
  • Docs:
    • lasR: https://r-lidar.github.io/lasR/ and https://github.com/r-lidar/lasR
    • lidR: https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=lidR and https://r-lidar.github.io/lidRbook/
    • PDAL EPT reader: https://pdal.io/en/stable/stages/readers.ept.html
  • Open questions: can EPT node tiles be merged and fed to {lasR} or lidR directly; are COPC versions of these projects available.

Option 3: try gloBFPr and compare against the lidar DSM (needs discussion)

Install gloBFPr into a temporary library and compare its building heights and fused DSM with the lidar surface and OSM-tagged heights for known buildings (City Hall, 100 Light Street, the tall towers).

  • Pros:
    • One call (search_3dglobdf()) returns footprints and heights for every building in a bounding box, so coverage is complete, with no large download.
    • Includes a canopy height model ("metachm" or "ethCHM") through get_fused_dsm(); get_3d_world() can build 3D scenes.
    • Actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-04); on CRAN as 2.0.0 on 2026-11-05 although the README still says “soon”.
  • Cons:
    • Heights are modeled (GlobalBuildingAtlas RMSE 1.5 to 8.9 m across continents; North America not broken out in what was read).
    • get_fused_dsm() gives each building one flat roof height, so the City Hall dome and tower tops would be lost.
    • The DEM comes from OpenTopography and needs an API key; 3DEP 1 m access is restricted to academic accounts. get_fused_dsm() has no dem argument (get_3d_world() does), so a terrainr DEM could not be used there.
    • Licenses are mixed: GlobalBuildingAtlas polygons are ODbL but heights and LoD1 models are CC BY-NC 4.0, which may rule out some uses.
    • Dataset vintage versus 2026 is unknown; experimental lifecycle.
  • Docs:
    • https://github.com/billbillbilly/gloBFPr
    • 3D-GloBFP data: https://zenodo.org/records/15487037
    • GlobalBuildingAtlas paper: https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/17/6647/2025/
    • GlobalBuildingAtlas LoD1 Parquet: https://source.coop/walkthru-earth/indices/building
    • OpenTopography API key: https://portal.opentopography.org/requestService?service=api

Comparison (for discussion)

1. Lidar DSM 2. R tooling for lidar 3. gloBFPr
Roof detail (domes, spires) Yes Yes No (flat roofs)
Post-2014 buildings No (patch from OSM) No (patch from OSM) Depends on dataset vintage
Trees Yes, leaf-off Yes, leaf-off Canopy model (metaCHM)
Height source Measured Measured Modeled
Effort and size Large download Large download Small
External dependency Python R only ({lasR} off CRAN) R; OpenTopography key
Tested here Yes (500 m window) No No

A possible hybrid, to discuss: lidar DSM as the base, OSM heights to patch newer buildings, and gloBFPr as a cross-check and gap filler.

Related footprint packages (for completeness)

  • {geomorphR} (CRAN 0.2.1, updated 2026-10): extract_geometric_features() for per-footprint shape metrics and compare_footprints(), which compares two periods by intersection-over-union and returns new construction and demolitions. Could flag buildings added or removed since the lidar year so only those need an OSM height patch. Needs a footprint layer for the earlier period (e.g. derived from the lidar surface or the old City dataset). It does not estimate heights.
  • {foot} (WorldPop; GPL-3; not on CRAN; last updated 2022-06): building morphology metrics (area, shape, orientation, nearest-neighbor distance, clustering) for 2D footprints, plus tiled reading and writing. No heights, so low relevance here.
